messages.subject: Re: repeated sampling in a season
messages.body_plain:
Yes - if you just want to pool April and May data to increase sample
size, then record all detections for each point, regardless of which
visit the detection was made, then either record effort for each point
as 2 or add an overall multiplier (or rather 'divider') of 2.  (The
former approach is usually preferred, in case not all points were
visited the same number of times.)

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Line transect/effort questions
messages.body_plain:
David Stroppel wrote:
> > I have conducted line transect surveys for grassland birds using transects

> > with an unequal number of repetitions/effort.
> >
> > I understand that I could use a multiplier that would act globally across

> > all transects if survey effort was equal)
> >
> > 1. To adjust for varying number of repetitions/effort am I correct that I

> > can do one of the following two things.
> >

> > One, I could just enter the transect length as the length times the number
> > of visits, ex) 300m * 10 visits = 3000m length. In this way Distance would
> > know that I surveyed from 3000m of transects and not 300m and could adjust
> > the density estimates accordingly.
> >
Yes, that is correct.  However, unequal number of repetitions raises
other issues.  If for example the number of times you covered a line was
correlated with bird density, that will bias density estimates.  e.g. if
you cover lines more times where there are lots of birds, you would
overestimate global density.

> > Two, I could enter the length (300m) and add a field for the number of

> > reps/effort and then multiply transect length by this new effort field.
> >

Yes.  Note however that the column under line transect states 'survey
effort', not 'line length', so that could be a misleading way to code
your data, should others use your project file.

> > 2. Am I correct that Distance cannot do model averaging across covariates

> > that I add such as burn year?
> >

> > I've had some models within two AIC units of each other and would like to

> > do some model averaging within Distance rather than in another program or

> > by hand.
> >
I don't think you can fully automate this in Distance.  You can do model
averaging by specifying multiple models, and then choosing the bootstrap
option to estimate variance, so that model uncertainty is accounted
for.  In your case, you could write code to do model averaging, e.g.
using AIC weights, reading results from a Distance output file.  See the
section on 'exporting MCDS results'.

> > 3. I have three possible burn years (2005, 2006, 2007) and I see that the

> > parameter estimate for 2007 is included in the intercept. How do I get the

> > parameter estimate for this burn year?
> >

These are relative estimates.  So the 2005 estimate is an estimated
difference, taking 2007 as the reference year.  You can change the order
to change the reference year.  If the 2005 and 2006 parameters are zero,
then you're estimating absolute effects for 2007.  If you include the
2005 coefficient in your model, then you're estimating absolute effects
for 2005, and similarly for 2006.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Autocorrelated transects?
messages.body_plain:
Imagine you are designing a survey with 2 strata using systematically placed
parallel lines. One stratum receives double the coverage of the other. All
transects will be oriented in the same direction. Would it be correct to
place a single transect grid over the entire survey area, but only fly every
second transect in the low coverage stratum? The advantage of doing this
would be less ferrying time, as the transects are contiguous across strata.
But this is what worries me. Is there an autocorrelation issue if a single
transect crosses 2 strata in a contiguous way, and is flown in one go but
divided into 2 transects for analysis?

Hoping this question is comprehensible,

Daniel Pike.

messages.body_plain:
Ray:

Here are my brief answers to your questions.

> > 1) What are the most important drawbacks of using a negative exponentia=
l=20
> > model for estimating animal abundance?=20
> >  =20
You know that f(0) plays a fundamental role in the estimation of=20
abundance or density using distance sampling.  It is defined as the=20
value that the probability density function takes on at distance zero. =20
Thinking about the geometry of the negative exponential, you will=20
realize that the rapid drop off of a negative exponential function in=20
the vicinity of distance zero will result in a very sensitive estimate=20
of f(0).  That is why Buckland et al. (2001) speaks about a shoulder=20
criterion; the desire to have the probability density function changing=20
very slowly (or not at all) for some distance away from the transect line.

It is very commonly the case that the negative exponential model results=20
in a overestimation of abundance or density; this is because the=20
estimate of f(0) derived from the negative exponential is too large,=20
leading directly to the positive bias in the abundance or density estimat=
e.
> > 2) Can those drawbacks be overcome, or should one ALWAYS use hazard rat=
e,=20
> > uniform, or half normal models instead?
> >  =20
"Always" and "never" terms are inadvisable to offer for any statistical=20
procedure.  However, in my opinion, I would not use the negative=20
exponential model because reviewers of your work will scrutinize your=20
findings more rigorously than if you applied the less erratic detection=20
function models.
> > 3)  Do you agree that large sample sizes make it HARDER to find =93good=
 fit=94=20
> > when conducting a Chi Square Goodness of Fit test? (i.e., if you increa=
se=20
> > the sample size so that you maintain a constant distribution of distanc=
e=20
> > values, p will decrease, making you more likely to find a significant=20
> > difference between your data and your model, thus more likely to FAIL t=
o=20
> > find goodness of fit.).
> >  =20
Increase in data will increase the power of any test.  Goodness of fit=20
tests contrast data with a model, and as we know all models are wrong=20
(but some are useful).  With enough information we discover that any=20
model is flawed.
> > 4) What is the most important method of evaluating goodness of fit?
> > a) the plot of your model and your data
> > b) Qq plot
> > c) Chi-square or Kolmogorov-Smirnov test
> >  =20
For ungrouped data, a QQ plot give a visual assessment of the congruence=20
of prediction with observation (i.e., model fit).  It is a very useful=20
diagnostic tool that you can use to scrutinize your data for=20
pathologies.  It is superior to your item (a) because it is not=20
dependent upon bin widths, which are subjectively chosen.  However, QQ=20
plots do not provide numerical assessment or quantification of fit. =20
That comes from statistical tests you describe in (c).  Note that in (c)=20
you have the chi-square (again dependent upon subjective decisions about=20
bin widths), and the K-S test that is not dependent upon bin widths. =20
Also note there are the Cramer-Von Mises tests available in distance=20
that resemble the K-S test because they do not require binning.  The=20
weighted version of the Cramer-Von Mises test acknowledges that=20
behaviour of the model nearer the transect line is more important than=20
model performance away from the transect line (because of the f(0)=20
argument above).

--=20

messages.subject: Re: Detections without a distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

You are right that Distance does not include observations with missing=20
distances in its analyses -- in fact they are weeded out by the routine=20
that extracts data from the Distance project database and sends it off=20
to the analysis engines -- so the analysis engines never see these=20
observations.  So, in the standard analyses Distance performs, it is=20
just as if you had never recorded these observations in the first place.

What is the effect of this?  If any of these observations are on the=20
line, then you are violating the assumption that all animals on the line=20
are detected (and recorded).  However, in that case, I guess you would=20
have the distance!  If they are off the line, then you are simply=20
missing animals off the line, which is perfectly acceptable in distance=20
sampling.  The more you miss, the steeper the decline in "detectability"=20
(ie detection, identification and recording distance) as you go away=20
from the line, but so long as this decline doesn't get too steep it's no=20
big deal.  If you miss lots of birds close to the line, you may have=20
problems with a small shoulder -- you therefore need to focus on getting=20
distance measurements for birds on and close to the line.

Your qq plot got stripped out of the message you sent to the list=20
(attachments are not allowed, to prevent viruses), so I can't comment=20
much.  Anyway, as you now know, the observations without distances do=20
not appear on this plot. It does sound from your description, however,=20
as if you have lots of observations at zero distance.  Have a look in=20
the Distance online help index for "Qq-Plots" and look at the figure on=20
the help page - the figure caption is "Example qq plot, showing a severe=20
=91spike=92 at 0 distance".  If your plot looks a bit like this, you have=
=20
quite a problem.  Possibly, if the observers recorded radial distance=20
(with the rangefinder) and angle from the line, you have a problem of=20
rounding of angles to 0.  Data with this problem are hard to salvage --=20
I expect it's been discussed previously on the list, and there's=20
material in the survey design and field methods part of the Intro to=20
Distance Sampling book on how to prevent it happening in future.

Hope this helps,

  - Len Thomas
